lessons.title: The purpose and principles of pest inspection
lessons.html:
Inspection drives everything

In integrated pest management, the inspection is the foundation of every decision. A treatment plan based on a poor inspection will target the wrong pest, the wrong place or the wrong cause, wasting chemicals and the client's money and often failing completely. A thorough inspection answers five questions: What pest is present? Where is it living and feeding? How many are there and how widespread is the infestation? Why is it there, in terms of food, water, shelter and entry points? What risks does the site present for treatment?

Types of inspection

  • Initial or survey inspection for a new client or a new complaint, establishing the baseline.
  • Routine monitoring inspections under a service contract, for example monthly in a food factory or grain silo.
  • Pre-treatment inspection to plan a specific intervention such as a fumigation.
  • Post-treatment or follow-up inspection to confirm efficacy.
  • Statutory or transactional inspections, such as wood destroying insect inspections for property transfers where these are required by the parties or local practice, and phytosanitary inspections for export.

Principles

  1. Systematic coverage: follow a set route so no area is missed, typically outside perimeter first, then inside, from high to low and room by room.
  2. Think like the pest: know the habits of likely pests and search where they hide, such as wall voids, under equipment, behind skirting, in roof spaces and in grain residues.
  3. Look for evidence, not only live pests: droppings, rub marks, gnaw marks, frass, cast skins, webbing, damage, tracks, odours and dead specimens.
  4. Identify conditions conducive to pests: spillage, poor sanitation, moisture, clutter, gaps and poor stock rotation.
  5. Record objectively: facts, locations and quantities rather than impressions.
  6. Inspect safely: assess site hazards before entering.

lessons.title: Planning and conducting the inspection
lessons.html:
Before arriving on site

  • Review the client's request, history, previous reports and trap data.
  • Agree access times, areas and the client contact who will accompany you.
  • Confirm site rules: induction, food safety requirements such as no jewellery and hairnets, permits for confined spaces or working at height.
  • Prepare equipment.

Inspection equipment

ItemUse
Bright torch and inspection mirrorDark voids, behind and under equipment
Hand lens or magnifierInsect identification, frass, eggs
Specimen vials and labelsCollecting samples for identification
Probe, screwdriver or moisture meterTesting timber for soundness and moisture
Sieve, tray and grain probeStored product inspection
Camera, site plan, checklistRecording findings and locations
PPEDust mask, gloves, overalls, hard hat, knee pads as needed

Conducting the inspection

  1. Meet the client contact and ask about sightings, complaints and recent changes.
  2. Inspect the exterior: perimeter, vegetation against walls, drainage, refuse areas, entry points around doors, pipes and vents, bird roosting sites, rodent burrows.
  3. Inspect the interior systematically, including roof voids, ceilings, wall junctions, storage, production areas, under and behind equipment, drains and staff areas.
  4. Check existing monitoring devices, such as bait stations, insect light traps and pheromone traps, and record activity.
  5. Collect specimens where identification is uncertain.
  6. Photograph evidence with a reference to location.

Safety during inspection

Never enter roof spaces, crawl spaces, silos or bins without assessing the hazards: fragile ceilings, electrical wiring, heat, moving machinery, engulfment in grain, and residual fumigant gas. Use lockout and confined space procedures where they apply, and never work alone in high-risk areas.

lessons.title: Recording, reporting and recommending
lessons.html:
The inspection report

The report is the product the client sees and it often becomes an audit document. It must be accurate, clear and actionable.

Contents of a good report

  • Client, site, date, time and inspector, including registration details where relevant.
  • Areas inspected and areas not accessible, with reasons. Inaccessible areas must be stated so that the client understands the limits of the inspection.
  • Pests identified, with evidence type, location and level of activity.
  • Conducive conditions found, such as hygiene, structural and storage issues.
  • Risk assessment: health, product contamination, structural damage or regulatory risk.
  • Recommendations, separated into client actions (sanitation, proofing, repairs, stock rotation) and pest management actions (monitoring, treatment method, products to be considered).
  • Photographs and a site plan marking findings.

Measuring activity

Use consistent scales so trends can be tracked over time, for example none, low, moderate or high activity, or counts per trap per week. Trend data from routine inspections shows whether control is working and supports decisions on intervention thresholds.

Communicating findings

Discuss significant findings with the client contact before leaving. Explain risks without exaggeration and give practical recommendations. For urgent findings, such as rodents in a food production area or live insects in grain intended for export, notify the responsible manager immediately so they can protect product and meet their obligations.

Professional integrity

Report what you find, not what the client hopes to hear. Do not recommend unnecessary treatments. Keep copies of reports and data according to company and legal requirements.

Key points

  • Inspection identifies what, where, how many, why and what risks before any treatment decision.
  • Inspect systematically and look for evidence and conducive conditions, not only live pests.
  • Prepare equipment, site rules and safety controls before arriving.
  • State inaccessible areas and record activity on consistent scales.
  • Separate client actions from pest management actions in recommendations.
